## Introduction and overview {#intro}

  ----------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Module                  Advanced Graph Neural Networks
  Code                    Not communicated — module announced by the master's brochure; SynapseS 2026-2027 sheet not published (the S3/S4 tracks of the catalog are currently empty).
  Team and workload       LLGA team (École Polytechnique) · teaching hours and ECTS not communicated · the “research” continuation of the Graph ML module (M1 P2): expressive power and the Weisfeiler-Lehman test, over-squashing, positional encodings, graph transformers, temporal GNNs, robustness — up to industrial scale and the laboratory's research.
  Period                  M2 · period 1 (brochure)

**Audience**: an engineer who has already trained a GCN/GAT (M1 Graph ML) and seen accuracy stall with depth, or two isomorphic molecules scored identically. **Empirical first**: over-squashing on a bottleneck; 1-WL failing to separate two regular graphs — then we name expressive power, PE, graph transformers.

Research follow-up to M1 Graph ML: WL, over-squashing, encodings, graph transformers, temporal, scale, robustness. Official sheet unpublished — this material deepens the brochure and flags additions.

### What you will be able to do

-   Determine the expressive power of a GNN via the Weisfeiler-Lehman test and deduce what it cannot distinguish.
-   Diagnose over-squashing in deep GNNs and choose the appropriate remedies.
-   Choose a positional or structural encoding depending on the task and the graph.
-   Decide between a message passing GNN and a graph transformer, and justify the choice.
-   Handle dynamic and temporal graphs.
-   Scale a GNN: sampling, systems and trade-offs.
-   Analyze the robustness and privacy specific to relational data.
-   Situate the open bridges: 3D, algorithmic reasoning, GNN × LLM.

### Where this course fits in the program

An M2 module (period 1), whose official teaching volume is not communicated. It builds directly on the message passing foundation of [Graph Machine and Deep Learning for Generative AI](../m1p2-graph-ml/index.html) (M1 P2), reactivated in chapter 0. Downstream, it prepares [Graph Generative Models and Applications](../m2-graph-generative-models/index.html), which builds graphs rather than analyzing them, and [Fundamentals of Security and Robustness for AI](../m2-security-robustness/index.html), whose adversarial attacks on graphs — like Nettack — extend the robustness chapter.

### Course outline

-   **Background: the message passing foundation** — the M1 base GNN restated, to expose its limits.
-   **Expressive power: the Weisfeiler-Lehman test** — the exact bound of what a standard GNN can distinguish.
-   **Over-squashing and deep GNNs** — why information compresses poorly in deep architectures, and how to remedy it.
-   **Positional and structural encodings** — giving the graph what transformers have beyond message passing.
-   **Graph transformers** — attention applied to vertices: promises, costs and conditions of use.
-   **Dynamic and temporal graphs** — handling structures that evolve over time.
-   **Scale: sampling, systems** — making training fit on industrial graphs.
-   **Robustness and privacy on graphs** — attacking and defending models whose data is relational.
-   **Research at DaSciM (Vazirgiannis, Lutzeyer)** — the laboratory's papers, read with the module's grid.
-   **LLGA bridges: 3D, algorithmic reasoning, GNN × LLM** — where this research meets the master's other axes.
-   **Exercises** — expressiveness tests, encodings and scaling to carry out yourself.
-   **References** — the research papers underlying each chapter.

### How to study this module

-   First secure the foundation: the review chapter 0 conditions everything else in the module.
-   Implement the Weisfeiler-Lehman test on small graphs: nothing makes expressive power as concrete as two indistinguishable graphs.
-   Read each founding paper after the corresponding chapter: the course is its map, not its substitute.
-   Connect the robustness chapter to the M2 security module: Nettack and its successors are studied there for their own sake.
-   Experiment with scaling on large datasets, and measure what sampling costs in quality.
-   Explore the bridges of the last chapter: this is where internship and PhD topics are recruited.

[Extrapolons note]{.tag} Graph half of the master, up to the GNN × LLM crossroads. Research (PhD, research engineer) or large-scale industrial GNNs: diagnose expressive power / over-squashing before stacking layers.
:::

## 0. Background: the message passing foundation {#ch0}

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Review of the Graph ML module (M1 P2) — what is assumed known
:::

-   **Generic layer** (M1, ch. 5): $h_v^{(\ell+1)} = \phi\big(h_v, \mathrm{AGG}_{u \in \mathcal{N}(v)}\{\psi(h_v, h_u)\}\big)$; GCN (renormalized averaging, spectral derivation), GraphSAGE (sampling, inductive), GAT (edge attention);
-   **Spectral** (M1, ch. 4): Laplacian $L = D - A$, variational characterization of $\lambda_2$, spectral clustering as a RatioCut relaxation, convolution by Chebyshev polynomials — filtering = a polynomial of $L$;
-   **Embeddings** (M1, ch. 3): DeepWalk/node2vec and their NetMF reading (factorization of random-walk matrices); the PathNNs of ch. 8 are their generalization;
-   **Link prediction / GAE** (M1, ch. 6) and **scale** (M1, ch. 7: NeighborSampler, Cluster-GCN, GraphSAINT) — the ch. 6 below extends the latter;
-   **Over-smoothing** (M1, ch. 5): after many layers, all embeddings converge (proved on a regular graph: geometric convergence to the mean) — why one stops at 2-4 layers… and why this module exists.
::::

::: note
[The module's four research questions]{.tag} (1) *How far can a GNN see?* — expressive power (ch. 1); (2) *How far can information travel?* — over-squashing and depth (ch. 2); (3) *Where am I in the graph?* — position and structure (ch. 3); (4) *At what scale and under what attacks?* — systems (ch. 6) and robustness (ch. 7). Transformers (ch. 4) and the temporal dimension (ch. 5) answer "all-all" and "as time goes by" to these same questions.
:::

## 1. Expressive power: the Weisfeiler-Lehman test {#ch1}

Concrete scene: two non-isomorphic 6-regular graphs. Your 3-layer GCN produces the same embeddings (up to perm) — link-pred AUC \~0.5. Not an implementation bug: the 1-WL bound. This chapter makes it operational *before* stacking gadgets.

::: note
[What breaks]{.tag} Believing a deeper GNN "sees more" (often false); evaluating on graphs 1-WL already separates (false sense of power); ignoring initial features (they fix the colors). All three sabotage paper-reading as much as a molecular toy.
:::

::: def
[Definition 1.1 — 1-WL (color refinement)]{.tag} Initialize a color $c_v^{(0)}$ from the features; iterate: $$c_v^{(k+1)} = \mathrm{HASH}\Big(c_v^{(k)},\ \mathrm{SORT}\big\{c_u^{(k)} : u \in \mathcal{N}(v)\big\}\Big).$$ Two graphs are *1-WL-equivalent* if the multisets of colors coincide at convergence. 1-WL distinguishes *almost all* random graphs (Babai-Erdős-Selkow); but fails on simple families: regular graphs of the same degree, cycles, pairs of molecules discussed since the 1960s (CIR: chemical identity recognition).
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 1.2 — GNN ≤ 1-WL (Xu et al., 2019; Morris et al., 2019)]{.tag} Any message passing GNN whose aggregation and update are functions (continuous, computable) cannot distinguish two 1-WL-equivalent graphs: if the initial colors coincide and the layers saturate the test, the embeddings coincide at every depth.

::: proof
By induction on $\ell$. Initialization: initial colors = features, identical by assumption, so $h_v^{(0)} = h_{v'}^{(0)}$ for every pair $(v, v')$ of the same color. Heredity: if all nodes of color $c$ have the same representation $h_c$, then the input of the aggregation at $v$ is the multiset $\{h_c : c \in \mathrm{multicol}_v\}$; now 1-WL-equivalence = equality of color multisets *and* of neighbor color multisets at each iteration — so AGG receives identical inputs, and $h_v^{(\ell+1)} = h_{v'}^{(\ell+1)}$. In the end, the readouts (permutation-invariant by construction, M1 ch. 2) see only the multiset of the $h_v$ — identical on both graphs. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: thm
[Theorem 1.3 — GIN reaches exactly 1-WL (Xu et al., 2019)]{.tag} With sum + MLP and discrete features, $$h_v^{(k+1)} = \mathrm{MLP}^{(k)}\Big((1 + \epsilon^{(k)})\, h_v^{(k)} + \sum_{u \in \mathcal{N}(v)} h_u^{(k)}\Big)$$ the GNN distinguishes exactly what 1-WL distinguishes.

::: proof
The ingredient: on a countable domain, there exists an *injective* function $f : \text{finite multisets} \to \mathbb{R}$: encoding each element by an integer (canonical log of a prime: $c \mapsto \log p_c$) gives $\sum_i \log p_{c_i}$, and the uniqueness of prime factorization ensures injectivity; a universal MLP approximates it. Then the sum+MLP layer is injective in $(h_v, \mathrm{multiset}(h_u))$ — the pair (own color, neighbor multiset) is encoded without collision: by induction, two nodes have the same embedding $\iff$ same 1-WL color. The injective sum readout concludes: GIN = 1-WL. [∎]{.qed}
:::

Immediate consequences: mean and max are *not* injective — $\{a, a, a\}$ and $\{a\}$ have the same mean; $\{a, a\}$ and $\{a\}$ the same max — so GCN/GraphSAGE (mean) are *strictly less* powerful than GIN on categorical features; in practice the difference shows up mainly on tasks where *counting* neighbors matters (molecules: $\mathrm{CH}_4$ vs $\mathrm{CH}_3$-$\mathrm{CH}_3$).
::::

::: ex
[Example 1.4 — C6 vs 2×C3: 1-WL fails, 2-WL separates (demonstration)]{.tag} *1-WL*: all nodes have degree 2; by induction, at each round each node sees (its color, {its color, its color}) — the colors remain uniform on each graph, and identical *between* the two graphs: indistinguishable. *2-WL* (pair coloring): consider an adjacent pair $(u, v)$. In the triangle, $\{w : w \sim u, w \sim v\}$ counts 1 common vertex; in C6, this count is 0 (no triangles); the 2-WL update rule, which aggregates for the pair $(u,v)$ the colors of the pairs $(u, w)$ and $(w, v)$ for all $w$, encodes the number of triangles — the pair histograms differ: separated. [∎]{.qed} Moral: 2-WL (hence a 2-GNN) "counts the moments" that the local sum cannot see. To code in the lab (exercise 1).
:::

::: thm
[k-WL and k-GNN hierarchy]{.tag} **k-WL** colors *k-tuples* of nodes: $k = 2$: pairs (above); the hierarchy is strict: (k+1)-WL distinguishes pairs that k-WL confuses (for $k \geq 1$, 2-WL already being strictly stronger than 1-WL); at the top, k = n+1 → exact isomorphism test (exponential). The **k-GNNs** (Morris et al., 2019) implement (a local variant of) k-WL: messages between neighboring k-tuples — memory and compute cost $\mathcal{O}(n^k)$: k = 2 practical, k = 3 reserved for small graphs (molecules). Morris et al.'s survey (2023) draws the complete map (Weisfeiler-Lehman "go machine learning").

  Model                    Power                                     Cost
  ------------------------ ----------------------------------------- -----------------------
  GCN / GraphSAGE (mean)   < 1-WL                                   $\mathcal{O}(\|E\|)$
  GIN (sum+MLP)            = 1-WL                                    $\mathcal{O}(\|E\|)$
  PathNN (ch. 8)           strictly > 1-WL (simple paths)           sampled
  GOAT (ch. 8)             strictly > invariants (learned orders)   $\mathcal{O}(\|E\|)$
  2-GNN / 2-WL             counts triangles, separates regular       $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$
  3-GNN                    cycles, most molecules                    $\mathcal{O}(n^3)$
:::

::: thm
[Pragmatic alternatives: subgraphs and motif counting]{.tag}

-   **ESGNN** (Equivariant Subgraph Aggregation, Bevilacqua et al., 2022): each node is described by the collection of subgraphs (ego-nets of increasing radius, or "node-deletion" — the graph deprived of $v$); a shared 1-WL GNN encodes them, aggregation across subgraphs adds expressive power *without* full $\mathcal{O}(n^k)$ cost — strictly between 1-WL and 3-WL;
-   **Motif counting** (Bouritsas et al., 2020): precompute counts of isomorphic subgraphs (triangles, paths, cycles) and inject them as features — "moments matter": raising expressive power by preprocessing rather than by architecture; direct link with Example 1.4 (triangles) and with the MMDs of generative evaluation (M1, ch. 9.6);
-   **Practical limits**: more expressive power = more estimation variance and cost; on real benchmarks (Dwivedi et al., 2023), GIN vs GCN is decided by tenths — expressive power is the bottleneck only on *structural* tasks (counting, distinguishing) — cf. ch. 6.
:::

## 2. Over-squashing and deep GNNs {#ch2}

::: def
[Definition 2.1 — Over-squashing (Alon & Yahav, 2021) — formal definition via Jacobians]{.tag} Let $\mathcal{G}$ be the computation graph of a GNN; the influence of a node $u$ on the final representation of a node $v$ is measured by the **Jacobian** $\big\| \partial h_v^{(L)} / \partial h_u^{(0)} \big\|$. There is *over-squashing* when this quantity is crushed exponentially with the distance $d(u, v)$ — precisely, when the bound $\big\| \partial h_v^{(L)} / \partial h_u^{(0)} \big\| \leq c\, (f \, r(\lambda_{\max}))^{-d(u,v)}$ becomes small because the *radius of convergence* $r(\lambda_{\max})$ of the propagation (an increasing function of the largest eigenvalue of the propagation operator, e.g. $2\tilde L_{\mathrm{sym}} / \lambda_{\max}$) is close to 1: an exponentially large quantity of information ($\sim$ growth rate $\mu$ of the neighborhood) must pass through a *channel* that contracts exponentially fast. *Bottlenecks* (cut edges, bridges between communities) are the physical points of the phenomenon.
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 2.2 — The expansion / $\lambda_{\max}$ link (proof sketch)]{.tag} The edges crossed by the information from $u$ to $v$ form a cut; the "flow" of message passing across a cut is bounded by the conductance of the cut, itself controlled by the spectrum: by Cheeger (inverted for the top of the spectrum, Tanner's bound for $\lambda_{\max}$), a weak conductance forces a large $\lambda_{\max}$… that is, highly oscillating components which, in the Chebyshev recurrence (M1, ch. 4), make the factor $\big( \frac{\lambda_{\max}}{2} \big)^k$ diverge and crush the radius of convergence: *topological bottleneck ⇔ poor spectral conditioning*. Hence the two families of remedies: change the *topology* (rewiring, below) or change the *operator* (normalization, implicit propagation, ch. 2.4).
:::

::: thm
[2.3 — Discrete Ricci curvature and SDRF (Topping et al., 2022)]{.tag} The **Ollivier-Ricci curvature** of an edge $(u,v)$ compares neighborhoods by optimal transport: $$\kappa(u, v) = 1 - \frac{W_1(\mu_u, \mu_v)}{d(u, v)}, \qquad \mu_u = \text{uniform law on } \mathcal{N}(u),$$ $W_1$ = Wasserstein-1 distance (Optimal Transport module): "locally dense" edges (triangles) → large $\kappa$; bridges → negative $\kappa$. **Worked example** (by hand):

-   edge of a triangle: $\mu_u = \{\frac12 v, \frac12 w\}$, $\mu_v = \{\frac12 u, \frac12 w\}$; transport plan: keep $w$ (cost 0), transport $\frac12$ from $v$ to $u$ (cost 1) → $W_1 = \frac12$, $\kappa = +\frac12$;
-   edge of a hexagon C6: the best plan transports $v \to t$, $s \to u$ (cost 1 each) → $W_1 = 1$, $\kappa = 0$;
-   bridge edge between two triangles (barbell): the best plan pays $W_1 = \frac{1}{3}(1 + 1 + 3) = \frac53$, so $\kappa = -\frac23 < 0$ — the bridge is "hyperbolic": it is the bottleneck.

**SDRF** (Spectral-De-Ricci-Flattening): at each iteration, (1) find the edge $(u,v)$ of minimal curvature; (2) add the edge $(x, y)$ between two neighbors of the edge (not yet present) that *maximizes the sum of curvatures* — triangulate the bottleneck; (3) remove the edge of maximal curvature if it exceeds a threshold (avoid densification); effect: the curvature distribution flattens, $\lambda_{\max}$ drops, the bound of Definition 2.1 improves. *Looking at the graph as a geometric object* — curvatures, distances, volumes — is one of the field's great turns (cf. ch. 9 and the Geometric DL module).
:::

::: note
[DIGL — diffusion rewiring (Gasteiger et al., 2021)]{.tag} A "filtering" alternative: replace $A$ by $\tilde A = \mathrm{top}\text{-}k\big(\sum_{i=0}^{K} \beta_i T_i(L)\big)$ — a sparsified heat kernel (sum of Chebyshev polynomials, M1 ch. 4): each node gains "virtual" edges toward its multihop neighbors weighted by the diffusion; simple, differentiable, and the final GNN trains on the *rewired* graph. Comparison: SDRF is *topological* (local curvature, targeted additions); DIGL is *spectral* (global diffusion); both target $r(\lambda_{\max})$ — and both may destroy motif information: measure the trade-off in the lab (exercise 4).
:::

::: thm
[2.4 — Deep GNNs: APPNP and GCNII]{.tag} **APPNP** (Klicpera et al., 2019) separates *predicting* from *propagating*: a network (often simple) predicts $H = f_\theta(X)$; propagation follows personalized PageRank: $$Z^{(k+1)} = (1 - \alpha)\, \hat P\, Z^{(k)} + \alpha H, \qquad \hat P = \tilde D^{-1/2} \tilde A \tilde D^{-1/2}.$$ Fixed point: $Z^\* = \alpha \big(I - (1 - \alpha)\hat P\big)^{-1} H$ — the series expansion $\sum_{k} \alpha(1-\alpha)^k \hat P^k$ shows that the effective depth is *infinite* without stacking parameters; the teleport $\alpha H$ bounds the gains (like PageRank damping, M1 ch. 0) and kills over-smoothing (M1, ch. 5.3); $K$ iterations = truncation of the series. **GCNII** (Chen et al., 2020) makes GCN *truly* deep through two mechanisms: $$h^{(\ell+1)} = \sigma\Big( \big[(1-\gamma_\ell) I + \gamma_\ell \hat P\big]\big[(1-\beta_\ell) I + \beta_\ell W_\ell\big] h^{(\ell)} + \gamma_\ell \hat P h^{(0)} \Big)$$ — *initial residual* toward $h^{(0)}$ (the same remedy as APPNP's teleport) and *mapped identity* $(1 - \beta_\ell) I$ (as in ResNet); with $\beta_\ell$ increasing with depth, 64 layers become trainable. Positioning: rewiring (2.3) changes *the channel*; APPNP/GCNII change *the dynamics*; graph transformers (ch. 4) remove the bottleneck by making the channel all-all; over-smoothing (representation) and over-squashing (channel) remain two distinct limits that must be diagnosed separately.
:::

## 3. Positional and structural encodings {#ch3}

::: def
[Problem: GNNs "do not know where they are"]{.tag} Message passing is equivariant (M1, ch. 2): two nodes with isomorphic neighborhoods have the same embedding — correct… but insufficient: the *global position* (distance to the center, membership in a cycle, bridge role) is informative. Transformers had the same problem (token order) and solved it with positional encodings — we re-import the idea (and its pathologies).
:::

  Encoding              Principle                                 Notes
  --------------------- ----------------------------------------- --------------------------------------------------
  **LapEig**            eigenvectors of $L$                       graph Fourier (M1, ch. 4); sign/base ambiguities
  **RWPE / RWSE**       return probabilities of the walk          simple, robust, computed by hand below
  **SE(3)-invariant**   distances, angles, areas (3D molecules)   ch. 9; Geometric DL module
  Learned / *anchor*    distances to anchor nodes                 inductive — recommended in production

::: thm
[3.1 — LapEig: the ambiguities, and SignNet to lift them]{.tag} Taking $p_v = [u_2(v), \dots, u_k(v)]$ (coordinates of $v$ on the eigenvectors) suffers from three pathologies: (i) *sign*: $-u_i$ is also an eigenvector — two runs give opposite encodings; (ii) *basis*: if $\lambda_i$ is multiple, any rotation of the basis is admissible; (iii) *instability*: a small perturbation of the graph crosses the eigenvalues and makes the basis jump. **SignNet** (Lim et al., 2022) builds functions invariant to sign and basis: $$\rho(V) = h\Big( \sum_{i=1}^{k} \phi(v_i) + \phi(-v_i) \Big),$$ with $\phi, h$ MLPs: enforcing the parity $\phi(v) + \phi(-v)$ makes $\rho$ even (sign invariance), and the sum over the basis gives invariance under rotation; the completeness theorem (in the spirit of results on orbit invariants): SignNet *universally* represents the continuous functions invariant in the eigenvectors — the exact analogue of Deep Sets' "sort before sum" (ch. 1). In practice: LapEig + SignNet is the default PE of spectral graph transformers.
:::

::: ex
[Example 3.2 — RWPE computed by hand (and why it matters)]{.tag} The *random-walk positional encoding* (RWSE, Dwivedi et al., 2020) of a node $v$ is the vector of return probabilities $\big[ (P)_{vv}, (P^2)_{vv}, \dots, (P^K)_{vv} \big]$, $P = D^{-1} A$. Computation:

-   node of a triangle: $(P^2)_{vv} = \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{2} = \frac12$ (back-and-forths); $(P^3)_{vv} = 2 \times (\frac12)^3 = \frac14$ (going around the triangle, in both directions);
-   node of a hexagon C6: $(P^2)_{vv} = \frac12$ — *identical* (same back-and-forths); but $(P^3)_{vv} = 0$: a return of odd length requires an odd cycle, and C6 has none; the first "full tour" appears only at $k = 6$, with $(P^6)_{vv} = 2 \times (1/2)^6 = \frac{1}{32}$.

Now C3 and C6 are exactly the pair that 1-WL cannot distinguish (Example 1.4): the RWSE — a single scalar, $p_3$, suffices here ($\frac14$ versus $0$) — separates them *immediately*. Structural PEs "buy" expressive power at cost $\mathcal{O}(\|E\| K)$; this is why the winning models of positional benchmarks (ch. 4) systematically carry a PE.
:::

::: thm
[3.3 — SE(3) invariants for molecules, and the theory of positions]{.tag} In 3D (ch. 9), the encoding must respect rotations/translations/reflections: invariants = interatomic distances $\|x_i - x_j\|$, angles, dihedrals; it is the continuous version of the principle "use only what is invariant". The theoretical question: *how many* coordinates to inject without breaking isomorphism invariance? A perfect positional encoding should distinguish the nodes of a *regular* graph (where 1-WL is constant) while remaining invariant under automorphism — *canonical* encodings (canonical numbering) make the learning variance explode; the practical compromise: *relative* encodings (RWSE, anchor distances, the SPD bias of ch. 4) — never absolute coordinates.
:::

::: note
[The inductive vs expressive debate]{.tag} Positional encodings partially "break" equivariance — a delicate choice between positional information and invariance guarantees. In industry (evolving graphs), one favors *inductive* PEs (generalizable to new nodes/graphs — RWSE, anchoring); in chemistry, exact invariants dominate. Cross-reference: Graphormer's SPD bias (ch. 4) is a *relative* PE — the only category that survives both constraints.
:::

## 4. Graph transformers {#ch4}

::: def
[Idea: all-all attention + structural bias]{.tag} Global attention $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$ removes bottlenecks and over-squashing at once (ch. 2); but without an encoding of the graph, a transformer on features alone is *blind to structure*: the topology must be reinjected via (i) positional encodings (ch. 3) and (ii) additive *attention biases* in the scores — structure steers attention rather than masking it.
:::

::: thm
[4.1 — Graphormer (Ying et al., 2021) — the three structural encoders]{.tag}

1.  **centrality encoding**: an embedding of the degree (in/out if directed) added to the features — degree is the first "where am I";
2.  **spatial encoding**: a bias learned per shortest-path distance: $$\mathrm{Attention}(Q, K)_{ij} = \frac{q_i^\top k_j}{\sqrt{d}} + b_{\phi(d_{ij})}, \qquad d_{ij} = \mathrm{SPD}(i, j), \quad b_{\phi(\cdot)} \text{ learned (table)},$$ with a dedicated value for $d_{ij} = \infty$ (disconnected nodes); the bias is *additive before the softmax* — structure conditions attention;
3.  **edge encoding**: on the shortest path $i \rightsquigarrow j$, the mean of the embeddings of the crossed edges is added to the score — for molecules, the type of the bonds along the path matters.

Plus a global virtual node (connected to all) for the readout. Result: 1^st^ rank on OGB-LSC PCQM4M (3.7M molecules) at its release. Implementation:

```python
import torch, torch.nn as nn
from torch_geometric.utils import shortest_path_distance   # PyG >= 2.6 (or homemade BFS)

class GraphormerLayer(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d, h, max_spd=5):
        super().__init__()
        self.attn = nn.MultiheadAttention(d, h, batch_first=True)
        self.bias = nn.Embedding(max_spd + 2, h)     # b_phi table: SPD -> h heads
        self.ffn = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(d, 2*d), nn.GELU(), nn.Linear(2*d, d))
    def forward(self, x, spd):                       # spd: (n, n) integer distances
        b = self.bias(spd.clamp(max=5).long()).permute(2, 0, 1)  # (h, n, n)
        x = self.attn(x, x, x, attn_bias=b)[0] + x
        return self.ffn(x) + x
```

*PyG trick*: the per-head bias is built with an embedding table indexed by the distance matrix (exercise 5).
:::

::: thm
[4.2 — GPS (Rampasek et al., 2022): the two channels, layer by layer]{.tag} $$H^{(\ell+1)} = \mathrm{MLP}\Big( \mathrm{BN}\big(\underbrace{\mathrm{MSA}(H^{(\ell)} + \mathrm{PE})}_{\text{global channel}} \;+\; \underbrace{\mathrm{MPNN}(H^{(\ell)}, A)}_{\text{local channel}}\big) \Big)$$ — *global* attention (all-all; kills over-squashing) + *local* message passing (locality bias, convolution); PE injected at the input (ch. 3); graph batches by concatenation-padding. Per-layer complexity: $\mathcal{O}(n^2 d)$ (attention) + $\mathcal{O}(\|E\| d)$ (MPNN) — the global channel dominates. GPS is a *recipe*: any MPNN (GCN, GINE, GAT) and any PE (RWSE, LapEig+SignNet) plug into it — hence its status as the reference framework.
:::

::: note
[4.3 — Efficient transformers: Exphormer and sampled attention]{.tag} For large $n$ (ogbn-products…), $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$ no longer fits; **Exphormer** (Shirzad et al., 2023) replaces full attention with a *sparse attention graph*: (i) the edges of the real graph; (ii) the neighbors of a random $d$-regular **expander graph** — an expander has logarithmic diameter: information crosses the graph in $\mathcal{O}(\log n)$ layers, precisely what ch. 2 demands (expansion!); (iii) global virtual nodes. Complexity linear in $n + \|E\|$; combined with the local MPNN, this gives "Exphormer-GPS", the scalable state of the art. Generalization: *sampled attention* (neighborhood, kernels, hashing) — the same recipes as the long-context transformers of the M2 LLMs module, transposed: the graph transformer and the LLM live the same algorithmic life.
:::

::: note
[4.4 — When is an MPNN enough? (decision guide)]{.tag}

-   *homophilous* graph, local dependencies (Cora, transactional fraud): GCN/GAT 2-3 layers — no point paying $n^2$;
-   motifs, distances, long-range dependencies (molecules, QA over KGs): transformer or ESGNN (ch. 1) — structure exceeds the neighborhood;
-   large $n$: MPNN + sampling (ch. 6) or Exphormer;
-   empirical benchmark rule (Dwivedi et al., 2023): at equal size, the gain of the transformer over MPNN+PE is real but modest — the hybrid (GPS) wins most often; the PE is the dominant factor, the architecture second.

LLGA connection: "attention = complete dynamic graph" versus "GNN = attention on a given graph" (M1, ch. 5); Graphormer is the synthesis — a *given* *and* learned attention — the transformers ↔ GNN convergence is THE guiding thread of the master.
:::

## 5. Dynamic and temporal graphs {#ch5}

::: def
[Two formalisms: snapshots vs event-based]{.tag}

-   **snapshots**: $G_1, G_2, \dots, G_T$ (graph aggregated per window); models: GCN+RNN (encode each snapshot, make recurrent); simple, but the granularity loses the order *within* the window;
-   **event-based**: the stream of timestamped interactions $(u, v, t_1), (u, w, t_2), \dots$ — the "true" formulation of the problem; it is the regime of fraud (millisecond) and sequential recommendation.
:::

::: thm
[5.1 — TGAT (Xu et al., 2020): encoding time]{.tag} The first notable event-based architecture injects time into attention: a learned sinusoidal temporal encoding (in the spirit of Time2Vec) $$\phi(\Delta t) = \big[\cos(\omega_1 \Delta t), \sin(\omega_1 \Delta t), \dots, \cos(\omega_d \Delta t), \sin(\omega_d \Delta t)\big], \qquad \omega_i \text{ learned},$$ concatenated with the features; attention is computed over the *strictly past* neighborhood $\mathcal{N}(v; t) = \{u : (u, v, t') \in E, t' \leq t\}$ — a causal GAT; inductive by construction (new nodes = new times).
:::

::: thm
[5.2 — TGN (Rossi et al., 2020): the modules and their equations]{.tag} TGN factorizes temporal memory:

1.  **memory** $s_i(t) \in \mathbb{R}^d$: a recurrent state per node, summarizing its history;
2.  **message**: at each event $(i, j, t)$, $m_i^t = \mathrm{msg}(s_i(t^-), s_j(t^-), \Delta t, e_{ij})$ (likewise for $j$, symmetric);
3.  **update**: $s_i(t) = \mathrm{GRU}\big(s_i(t^-),\ \mathrm{agg}(\{m_i^{t'} : t' \leq t\})\big)$ — only the nodes *touched by the batch* are updated; "at rest" nodes receive a placeholder message to age their memory;
4.  **embedding**: $z_i(t)$ computed by a TGAT-type module over the memory $\{s_u(t^-) : u \in \mathcal{N}(i; t)\}$ + the time encoding $\phi$ — memory is a *compressed summary*, the embedding an *attentive reading*.

Training: *strictly causal* — batches are ordered by time, and the *masked teacher forcing* technique (memorizing states between batches without backprop through the whole history, but "replaying" the stored states) makes the gradient practical; future link prediction loss: score $(i, j, t)$ against negatives (M1, ch. 6, temporal version). The paper's ablation: every module counts — remove memory, and everything collapses on distant interactions.
:::

::: note
[5.3 — LLGA application: real-time fraud]{.tag} The transaction graph is event-based by nature: a fraudulent card must be blocked in seconds; the pipeline: (i) TGN encodes the accounts (memory = past behavior); (ii) a head classifier reads $z_i(t)$ at the moment of the transaction; (iii) the *negatives* are old legitimate transactions — beware temporal contamination (train strictly before $t$: the temporal-split hygiene of the Emerging ML module); (iv) in production: incremental memory update, model drift to monitor. Lab datasets: Wikipedia edits / Reddit (TGN standards), and anonymized transaction banks. Variants: CAWN (attention by causal walks), compressed memorization; the state-of-the-art survey lives on the temporal graph learning side.
:::

## 6. Scale: sampling, systems {#ch6}

:::: recap
::: recap-title
What is assumed known (M1, ch. 7)
:::

NeighborSampler (fanouts, expansive neighborhood $1 + s_L(1 + s_{L-1}(\dots))$), Cluster-GCN (METIS partitioning, partition bias), GraphSAINT (subgraphs + bias-free coverage normalization), and the bias/variance/memory triangle. Here: the *systems* layer and experimental hygiene.
::::

-   **Multi-GPU and partitioning**: beyond one GPU, partition the graph (METIS/vertex-cut) across several machines; boundary edges are duplicated (shadow nodes) — the distributed training of the Emerging ML module applies almost as is (parameter server vs all-reduce); PinSage (M1, ch. 6) is the industrial reference;
-   **Caching and pipelining**: neighborhood sampling is a *system* problem (I/O, reuse of subgraphs across batches — hence PinSage's importance sampling that freezes the entry points); the frameworks: DGL, PyG + torch_geometric.sampler, Quiver;
-   **Summary of complexities**:
      Method            Memory/batch                          Bias        Notes
      ----------------- ------------------------------------- ----------- --------------------------
      full-batch        $\mathcal{O}(\|V\| + \|E\|)$         none        breaks beyond \~1M nodes
      NeighborSampler   $\mathcal{O}(\prod s_l)$            variance    inductive, standard
      Cluster-GCN       $\mathcal{O}(\|E\|/k)$               partition   deep possible
      GraphSAINT        $\mathcal{O}(\|\mathcal{G}_s\|)$   corrected   dense batches
-   **Benchmarks and hygiene**: OGB (ogbn-arxiv 169k; ogbn-products 2.4M; PCQM4M 3.7M molecules), public leaderboards; the "Benchmarking Graph Neural Networks" paper (Dwivedi et al., 2020/2023) sets the protocol: same parameter budgets, same splits, *multiple seeds with confidence intervals* — many "SOTAs" die by this yardstick; Bayesian hyperparameter search is the rule (gains < 0.5 point demanding a strict protocol);
-   **Good research practice**: always publish the variance, test significance (paired tests over seeds), and check for *leakage* (temporal splits for dynamic graphs — ch. 5).

## 7. Robustness and privacy on graphs {#ch7}

::: thm
[7.1 — Nettack (Zügner et al., 2018): gradient attack, in detail]{.tag} The scenario: *evasion* (the attacker modifies the graph at test time) on a target $u$ and its class $y_u$; budget: $\Delta$ modifications (edge additions/removals, feature changes). The attacker's dilemma: the model is not differentiable *in* the discrete structure. Nettack's solution:

1.  train a linearized *surrogate* (one-layer GCN, softmax); its output $Z_u(A)$ is then polynomial in $A$ — continuous, differentiable;
2.  **first-order score**: for each candidate modification $\delta$ (flip of an edge $(a,b)$ or of a feature), $$\mathrm{score}(\delta) = -\nabla_{A}\, \mathcal{L}_{att}\big(Z_u(A)\big)\big\|_{(a,b)} \cdot \big(\delta_{ab} - A_{ab}\big),$$ the Taylor approximation of the loss change (product of the gradient with the direction of the change); keep the modification with maximal score;
3.  iterate (modify, re-score) until the budget; "discretion" constraints: add only plausible edges (degrees, common features).

Historic result: a few flips suffice to flip the prediction — and the attacks *transfer* to the true GCN (the surrogate suffices). The LLGA lesson: in fraud detection, the attacker *knows* the model (or its shadow); robustness is a design requirement, not an option.
:::

::: thm
[7.2 — Poisoning: Meta-Self (Zügner & Günnemann, 2019)]{.tag} An attack *at training time* (poisoning): the graph is corrupted *before* learning. Bilevel: $$\min_{\delta}\ \mathcal{L}_{att}\big(f_{\theta^\*}(A + \delta)\big) \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \theta^\* = \arg\min_\theta \mathcal{L}_{train}\big(f_\theta(A + \delta)\big),$$ solved by *meta-gradient*: a few inner gradient steps are unrolled (differentiable), the outer gradient traces back to $\delta$ — the same machinery as the MAML of the RL/Deep Learning module. A "self-labeled" variant (Meta-Self): the attacker also controls a few labels. Structural defenses: **pruning** (attack edges are often "suspicious" — large feature distances); **purification** (Pro-GNN: learn a clean graph $A'$ regularized close to $A$ while training the GNN); **robust GCN** (RGCN, Zhu et al., 2019): Gaussian layers whose variance absorbs the attack + attention over reliable neighbors.
:::

::: note
[7.3 — Certification: sketch]{.tag} Guarantee that no attack of budget $\Delta$ changes the prediction: by *randomized smoothing* applied to graphs (majority over graphs perturbed by random flips) or by spectral bounds (certificates tied to $\lambda_{\max}$ of ch. 2 — same currency); the state of the art certifies small budgets on moderate GCNs: in practice, one combines partial certification + the defenses above + monitoring (detecting edge-addition anomalies).
:::

::: thm
[7.4 — Privacy: node-DP, edge-DP, reidentification]{.tag}

-   **edge-DP**: the basic mechanism is *randomized response* — flip each edge with probability $p$, calibrated for $(\varepsilon, 0)$-DP; counting queries (how many edges between two groups?) receive Laplace noise of sensitivity 1;
-   **node-DP**: much harder — sensitivity explodes with the degree (removing a node removes $d$ edges); recipe: *project* the graph onto a graph of bounded degree $k$ (keep the $k$ "most important" neighbors), then apply the edge mechanisms; the price: bias on hubs;
-   **reidentification**: graph embeddings (M1, ch. 3) are fingerprints — re-routing an "anonymized" node into a public graph by comparing neighborhoods (attacks by degrees, by subgraphs — the Narayanan-Shmatikov attack transposed); GraphRAG (M1, ch. 11) aggregates scattered facts: the reidentification risk *grows* with the quality of the graph;
-   **evaluation**: measure the utility-privacy trade-off (AUC vs $\varepsilon$); cross-reference with the M2 security module for LLMs (prompt injection over the KG, leakage by generation).
:::

::: note
[7.5 — Structural fairness]{.tag} Degree bias: low-degree nodes (minorities in social networks, new customers) are predicted less well — fewer messages = less signal; remedies: structural features (RWSE, ch. 3), virtual edges, degree-based resampling, reweighted losses; open question: *structural* fairness (communities) vs *individual* fairness (nodes) can conflict — the exact counterpart of the fairness tensions of the Optimal Transport module (transporting node distributions; homophily bias: a homophilous GNN propagates label biases).
:::

## 8. Research at DaSciM (Vazirgiannis, Lutzeyer) {#ch8}

The DaSciM laboratory (LIX, École Polytechnique — M. Vazirgiannis, J. Lutzeyer) is the master's host laboratory: this chapter studies its papers in depth, positioning them *relative to the program*. General-audience introductions were given in M1 (ch. 10); here we go into the machinery.

::: thm
[8.1 — Path Neural Networks, in depth (Michel, Nikolentzos, Lutzeyer & Vazirgiannis, ICML 2023)]{.tag} **Starting point**: the canonical GNN layer aggregates 1-hop neighbors (M1, ch. 5); stacking $L$ layers amounts — when all goes well — to aggregating *walks* of length $L$; but (i) walks *repeat* nodes (backtracking — redundant information); (ii) composing layers degrades (over-smoothing/squashing, ch. 2); (iii) 1-WL — hence the GNN (th. 1.2) — aggregates only multisets of colors, without the *sequence* of the route. **The path operator**: for each node $v$, enumerate *simple* paths (without repetition) starting from $v$, of length $\ell$; encode each path with a GRU, aggregate: $$m_p = \mathrm{GRU}\big(h_{u_\ell}^{(\ell)}, \mathrm{GRU}(\dots \mathrm{GRU}(h_{u_1}^{(0)}, h_v^{(0)}) \dots )\big), \qquad h_v^{(\ell)} = \mathrm{AGG}\big\{ m_p : p \in \mathcal{P}_v^{(\ell)} \big\}.$$ Three variants bound the enumeration cost:

-   **PathNN-s** (shortest paths): $\mathcal{P}_v$ = shortest paths to all destinations (at most $n - 1$ paths, $\mathcal{O}(n)$ GRUs per node); captures *distances* — two nodes "close to everyone" versus "peripheral" separate;
-   **PathNN-r** (random walks): $\mathcal{P}_v$ = sampled walks — the bridge with DeepWalk/NetMF (M1, ch. 3);
-   **PathNN-n** (neighborhood sampling): locally sampled simple paths — the practical compromise for large graphs.

**Complexity**: $\mathcal{O}(P \cdot \ell \cdot d^2)$ per node ($P$ sampled paths) — of the same order as a GAT if $P \sim \bar d$. **Results**: on graph classification (standard benchmarks including molecular ones — ZINC and TU datasets), PathNN matches or exceeds GIN/GCN; on tasks where *the geometry of routes* carries the signal (molecules: paths are chemical chains!), the gain is clear. **Theoretical positioning**: simple paths carry information that walk multisets ignore (recall: C6 vs 2C3, Example 1.4 — triangles are read in paths of length 3); *ordered* GRU aggregation is a special case of GOAT's "order + sequence" family (below); and PathNN is the subject of the "paper" exercise (exercise 7).
:::

::: thm
[8.2 — GOAT (Chatzianastasis, Lutzeyer, Dasoulas & Vazirgiannis, AAAI 2023)]{.tag} Seen in M1 (ch. 10) on the generation side; on the expressive power side: the invariant aggregator $\mathrm{AGG}$ (th. 1.2-1.3) bounds the GNN to 1-WL *precisely because it is invariant*; GOAT learns a **local order** by attention (scoring neighbors by $(h_v, h_u)$, sorting), then processes the sequence with an RNN — a sequence model *inside* the graph: strictly more expressive than invariant aggregation (it distinguishes identical distributions of a multiset as soon as the order carries signal), while remaining *globally* equivariant (the order is a learned function of the representations, not an external numbering). Positioning in M2: an *architectural* answer to the question of ch. 1 — gain expressive power without paying $\mathcal{O}(n^k)$; and an answer to ch. 3 — the local order is a *learned* positional encoding.
:::

::: thm
[8.3 — NGG (Evdaimon et al., 2024): conditioned latent generation]{.tag} The bridge M1-ch. 9 ↔ diffusion: a GNN encoder projects graphs into a compact latent space; a diffusion model (M1, ch. 9.5 — Multimodal GenAI) learns the distribution there *conditioned on structural features* (spectrum, degrees, counts); the decoder regenerates graphs exhibiting the requested features. The interest for M2: *latent* diffusion bypasses discretization (continuous diffusion in $\mathbb{R}^d$ rather than over DiGress's categories), and the spectral conditioning connects generation to ch. 2 (the spectrum governs communication — here, it governs the *shape* of the generated graphs). LLGA applications: faithful synthetic data (pre-training!), distributional anonymization, anomaly detection (a real graph far from the latent support).
:::

::: note
[8.4 — Pseudo-code prompting (Skianis, Nikolentzos & Vazirgiannis, 2024)]{.tag} Presented in M1 (ch. 11) as a GraphRAG tool; the M2 reading: a benchmark of *algorithmic reasoning* — LLMs execute graphs described in pseudo-code better than in natural language (systematic gains); to be connected with neural algorithmic reasoning (ch. 9): two ways of making algorithms run on graphs — by a prompted LLM, or by a trained GNN.
:::

## 9. LLGA bridges: 3D, algorithmic reasoning, GNN × LLM {#ch9}

::: thm
[9.1 — 3D molecules: EGNN and E(n) equivariance (Satorras, Hoogeboom & Welling, 2021)]{.tag} The positions $x_i \in \mathbb{R}^3$ make the molecular graph *geometric*; physics is invariant under rotations/translations (E(3)); a GNN that respects this symmetry *by construction* learns better with less data (Bronstein et al., the Geometric DL "charter"). EGNN: $$m_{ij} = \phi_e\big(h_i, h_j, \|x_i - x_j\|^2, e_{ij}\big),$$ $$x_i^{(\ell+1)} = x_i^{(\ell)} + C \sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}(i)} (x_i^{(\ell)} - x_j^{(\ell)})\, \phi_x(m_{ij}),$$ $$h_i^{(\ell+1)} = \phi_h\big(h_i^{(\ell)}, \textstyle\sum_{j} m_{ij}\big).$$ *Equivariance proof (sketch)*: under $x \mapsto Rx + t$ ($R$ orthogonal), the distances $\|x_i - x_j\|$ are invariant, hence so are the $m_{ij}$; the position step $\sum_j (x_i - x_j)\phi_x$ transforms into $R \sum_j (x_i - x_j)\phi_x$ — exact equivariance; the factor $C$ bounds the step. Applications: 3D property prediction, learned molecular dynamics, *3D generation* (EDM — equivariant diffusion; the M2 Geometric DL module generalizes to groups; M1 ch. 9 covers the 2D version).
:::

::: thm
[9.2 — Neural algorithmic reasoning (Veličković et al.)]{.tag} Learning to *execute* algorithms with GNNs: encode inputs as a graph (sorting: a list = a comparison graph; shortest paths: the graph itself), execute via message passing layers, decode outputs — the *black-box* replaces the code. The CLRS benchmark (Veličković et al., ICML 2023) tests faithful execution of classical algorithms (CLRS = Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein); results: GNN processors generalize to unseen sizes *better* than transformers on certain families (structural induction); the LLGA lesson: a learned algorithm is *differentiable* (it can be inserted into an end-to-end trained pipeline: routing, scheduling, matching) and *approximately robust* (noisy inputs); at the price of exactness — the trade-off to master. Loop with Refresher CS: what more can a "learned algorithm" do than an algorithm? Answer: train on data, slot into gradient descent — and the pseudo-code prompting of ch. 8.4 is the dual path (the LLM *simulates* the execution; NAR *embodies* it).
:::

::: thm
[9.3 — GNN × LLM: injected encoders and benchmarks]{.tag} Three injection architectures (M1, ch. 11.2, deepened):

-   **structural tokens**: the outputs of a GNN (node/graph embeddings) are projected into the LLM's embedding space as soft tokens; the LLM reads structure as a language;
-   **structural recall**: the GNN (or the graph traversal) retrieves the relevant facts, the LLM writes — RAG becomes "graph-RAG"; in both cases, the question of the *alignment* of the spaces arises (contrastive: bring the GNN embedding closer to the text describing the same node);
-   **LLM annotator**: the LLM enriches node features (summaries, types) for the GNN — the graph becomes text-attributed (the "TAG" regime); benchmarks: NLGraph (serialized reasoning — M1, ch. 11.2), Talk like a Graph (encodings: none dominates everywhere), and the industrial GraphRAG suites.

**Industrial GraphRAG** (summary; details in M1, ch. 11): LLM extraction → entity graph → Leiden communities + summaries → local/global queries; the M2's role: the *quality of the graph* (robust communities — ch. 7; KGC completion — M1 ch. 6) is the system's bottleneck; the rare specialty the master builds: both GNN theory *and* the LLM pipeline.
:::

::: note
[9.4 — What the master expects of you here]{.tag} Knowing how to choose: MPNN vs transformer (ch. 4), with or without PE (ch. 3), deep or rewired (ch. 2), certified or not (ch. 7) — and knowing how to *prove* the theorems of ch. 1, reproduce the experiments of ch. 8, and read a paper of the field in one hour. This is the "entry-level research / advanced R&D" level.
:::

## Exercises {#ex}

1.  **1-WL by hand.** Run 1-WL on C6 and 2×C3 and verify indistinguishability (detail Example 1.4); then on the "house" graph (square + roof) versus the pentagon; conclude on the exact family of indistinguishable pairs. *Partial solution*: house vs pentagon — all nodes of degree 2 except the roof top (degree 3); the pentagon is 2-regular, the house is not → 1-WL distinguishes them from iteration 1 (initial color = degree); generalization: 1-WL fails exactly on certain pairs of regular graphs with the same degree sequence (more finely: same iteration tree; connected 2-regular graphs = cycles, all indistinguishable from one another).
2.  **GIN vs GCN.** Show that the mean is not injective on multisets (give the counterexamples {a, a, a} vs {a} and {a, a, b, b} vs {a, b}) and that sum+MLP is (discrete features); check experimentally: train GIN and GCN on a 1-WL-indistinguishable pair and measure. *Partial solution*: mean: {a, a, a} → a and {a} → a (collision); discrete sum: encode a by $\log 2$, b by $\log 3$ — $\{a,a,b,b\} \mapsto 2\log 2 + 2\log 3 = \log 36$ and $\{a, b\} \mapsto \log 6$ — no collision by uniqueness of factorization (th. 1.3); in practice, the mean does better on continuous real features — discuss why (estimation variance).
3.  **Minimal 2-GNN.** Implement a 2-GNN on pairs (representation $h_{ij}$, messages between adjacent pairs) and verify that it separates C6 and 2C3 (disjoint readout outputs) where GIN fails. *Hint*: start with hashed colors (exact 2-WL) before learning.
4.  **Over-squashing.** Build two "communities" connected by a single bottleneck node; measure the classification performance of a GCN as a function of the distance to the bottleneck; compare GPS (ch. 4) and GCN + virtual edges (DIGL); plot $\lambda_{\max}$ before/after rewiring. *Partial solution (expected)*: gradient of accuracy with distance for the GCN; GPS nearly uniform; after DIGL, $\lambda_{\max}$ drops by several percent and the gap narrows — the $\lambda_{\max}$ vs accuracy curve is the graph to produce.
5.  **LapEig.** Compute the first 2 nontrivial eigenvectors of the Laplacian of the karate club graph; project the nodes; verify that the visualized separation ≈ the actual partition; rerun 5 times and observe the sign flips; implement the SignNet correction (ch. 3.1) and measure stability (distance between the encodings of two runs). *Partial solution*: $\rho(V) = \mathrm{MLP}(\sum_i \phi(v_i) + \phi(-v_i))$ — the sum of the two parities is invariant under flips; compare with the baseline "sign fixed by the first positive component" (unstable at nodes of near-zero value).
6.  **RWSE by hand and in code.** Recover the computations of Example 3.2 (triangle vs hexagon), then compute the RWSEs ($K = 4$) of all nodes of the karate club graph; show that two 1-WL-equivalent nodes of a regular graph get the same RWSE — and explain why this is both a *feature* (invariance under automorphism) and a *bug* (expressive power).
7.  **Graphormer-PE.** Implement the attention bias by shortest-path distance (distance matrix by BFS; learned bias table — skeleton in ch. 4.1); train on ogbg-molhiv and compare GCN / GIN / Graphormer-mini; report means ± standard deviations over 5 seeds. *Partial solution*: BFS $\mathcal{O}(n(\|V\| + \|E\|))$ per graph — precompute; clamp distances to 5 (Pareto law of molecular SPDs); expected: a small but systematic gain of the SPD bias over GCN.
8.  **Temporal.** On a standard TGN dataset (Wikipedia/Reddit): train a TGN (pytorch_geometric.nn.models.TGNMemory library or the paper's code); ablation: remove memory (keep the TGAT embedding); plot the AUC of future link prediction as a function of the horizon $\Delta t$. *Partial solution (expected)*: memory dominates on recent interactions; without memory, the AUC drops by several points at small $\Delta t$ (the information of the last events is no longer compressed).
9.  **Attack.** Implement an attack by removing/adding $k$ edges targeting a node (gradient over nonexistent edges — ch. 7.1, linearized surrogate); measure the prediction flip rate vs budget; test a defense (RGCN or training on perturbed graphs). *Partial solution*: score = \|gradient of the attack loss per edge\|; take the top-k; the surrogate suffices (transfer); with RGCN, the required budget roughly doubles — never zero; conclude on certification (ch. 7.3).
10. **Edge-DP.** Prove that randomized response (flipping each edge with probability $p$) is $(\varepsilon, 0)$-DP with $\varepsilon = \log \frac{p}{1-p}$ (analyze the two output mechanisms per edge); deduce the equivalent Laplace noise for an edge count. *Solution*: for two graphs neighboring in one edge, the likelihood ratio of any output is bounded by $\frac{p}{1-p}$ (worst case: the flipped edge); hence the $\varepsilon$; counting: each edge contributes Bernoulli($1-p$) vs Bernoulli($p$), the sum of $m$ Bernoullis has binomial noise — approximated by Laplace of variance $m\,p(1-p)$, i.e. scale $\sqrt{m\,p(1-p)}$.
11. **Research project.** Reproduce an experiment from one of (PathNN / GOAT / GPS / TGN / NGG) on OGB or TU; report: protocol, seeds, comparison to the published numbers, failure analysis — the M2's "paper" exercise; for PathNN: compare the three variants (s/r/n) on a molecular dataset and explain the observed hierarchy via ch. 8.1.
